definition: Conceptual clustering is a machine learning paradigm for unsupervised classification that has been defined by Ryszard S.
details: Michalski in 1980 (Fisher 1987, Michalski 1980) and developed mainly during the 1980s. It is distinguished from ordinary data clustering by generating a concept description for each generated class. Most conceptual clustering methods are capable of generating hierarchical category structures; see Categorization for more information on hierarchy. Conceptual clustering is closely related to formal concept analysis, decision tree learning, and mixture model learning.

explainer.lead: Conceptual clustering sorts unlabeled data while also explaining what each group means. Its concept descriptions make the resulting classes easier to interpret than clusters identified only by their members.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting a mixed box of toys without being told the categories. You might put toy cars together and describe them as “toys with wheels,” then group those with other vehicle toys. Conceptual clustering does something similar: it makes groups and gives each group a description.
tiers.practitioner: Use conceptual clustering when an unsupervised classification must include an interpretable description of every class, not just assignments to clusters. Inspect both the groupings and their descriptions, and check the category hierarchy produced by methods that support one; ordinary clustering alone does not provide the same output.
tiers.paperLevel: Given unlabeled data X, learn classes C_1, ..., C_k together with a concept description D_i for each class C_i; most methods can also generate hierarchical category structures. Ryszard S. Michalski defined the paradigm in 1980, and it was developed mainly during the 1980s. It is closely related to formal concept analysis, decision tree learning, and mixture model learning.

explainer.example: Given unlabeled customer-support tickets, a method could place password-reset and login-failure tickets in a class described as “account-access problems,” and late or missing deliveries in a class described as “delivery problems.” It could then place both classes beneath a broader “customer-support issues” category.

usedIn.name: Unsupervised classification
usedIn.detail: Creates classes from unlabeled data and supplies a concept description for each class.

usedIn.name: Hierarchical categorization
usedIn.detail: Most conceptual clustering methods can organize generated categories into hierarchies.

explainer.intuition: A useful category is more than a collection of similar items: it also has an explanation of what its members share. Conceptual clustering learns both the collection and that explanation.
howItWorks: Produce a concept description for each class.
Where supported, arrange categories into a hierarchy.
explainer.whyItMatters: The added descriptions connect unsupervised grouping with explicit concepts, making each generated class interpretable. Hierarchical category structures can also show how narrower and broader classes relate.
misconceptions: It is not simply ordinary clustering: every generated class also receives a concept description.
Its output need not be flat; most methods can generate hierarchical category structures.

nodes.label: Category hierarchy
nodes.note: A structure produced by most methods.
